title: Any advice on consistent pixel art and animations?
author: TalesofEternitydev
selftext: I'm primarily using claude code to make a game using pixel art but I'm having real trouble finding a way to create consistent game wide sprites and animations, I've decided to put it on the back burner while i continue to research and hope to one day hire a good artist but as of right now my game does look pretty trash when it comes to visuals and i would like to see if there's any advice you other ai devs can provide.

comments.author: Entropydemic
comments.body:
I would say have a base example of a sprite style, and then a base image to make for consistency. I personally use Gemini for this by first making a video. Aseprite is twenty bucks on Steam just one time, and it lets you cut from GIF or MPG (etc) and directly make sprite sheets. THEN if you want layering for weapons or clothing or hair... you can ask your tool to remake the sprite sheet with X changes. I recommend also making the background of your video blank or a bright opposing color to make it simpler to remove it in a single cut with Aseprite. The results are generally really cool sprite sheets, and if your game allows, heavily detailed (higher file size too) sprite sheets.

https://i.redd.it/z0atv242h4yh1.gif

replies.author: Entropydemic
replies.body:
This is another style, but using the same prompting method from video to sprite. Aseprite can also downscale it to a more pixelated form by pasting the images into smaller image constraints. (For example this into 128 by 128 pixels, etc)

https://i.redd.it/6hs4f0wjj4yh1.gif

comments.author: magic-studios-admin
comments.body: We published a free tool so you can experiment and tune yourself with your own GPU https://magicstudios.ai/welcome

comments.author: TraplineStudio
comments.body: Pick one canvas size and one palette first, say 32x32 with a palette from lospec.com, and run every sprite through the same last step that snaps it to that pixel grid and those colours. Most of the "doesn't belong together" look comes from mixed pixel sizes and colours, not from the drawings themselves.
